uncited: The 3D Ring Visibility & Occlusion Test is a screen-space rasterization technique used to determine which voxels are visible or occluded by the boundary segments of a 3D ring primitive.
It projects ring segments to screen space, computes depth via inverse-linear interpolation, and validates visibility against a voxel depth buffer.

It differs from sibling methods like [Change of Integration Variable for Boundary Segments](8107-change-of-integration-variable-for-boundary-segments.md) by operating in screen space using rasterization primitives rather than analytical integration in world space.
- Camera parameters: near plane distance $n$, focal length $f$, screen width $w$, screen height $h$, and basis vectors $\mathbf{right}, \mathbf{up}, \mathbf{forward}$.
- The ring is discretized into 3 segments (indices 0..2) and 32 sub-segments per ring (indices 0..31).
- Each sub-segment is defined by two endpoints in screen space.
Iterate over ring index $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and segment index $i \in \{0, \dots, 31\}$.
*(Note: The source implies a segment between two points, so let $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be the camera-space coordinates of the two endpoints of the segment.)*
If $\max(a_z, b_z) < n$, skip the segment.
If $\min(a_z, b_z) < n$, clip the segment to the near plane.
Compute bounding box $[x_{min}, x_{max}] \times [y_{min}, y_{max}]$ covering the segment.
Update voxel masks (`support`, `visible`, `definite`, `possible`, `edge`, `contact`) based on depth comparison and stroke status.
- Near clipping is handled by checking min/max z against the near plane and interpolating the cut point.
- Division by zero in depth calculation is avoided by using $\max(\text{near}, \dots)$.
